For particular ages and individuals, time outs definitely do work. Your job isn't done there, though. If looked at as a purely punitive action, you're likely to have less success. As equally as important as the consequence (in this case a time out) is the "processing" that occurs at the end of the time out.

"Why are you in time out?"

"What could you have done differently to avoid time out?"

"What will you do the next time the same situation arises?"

"What will happen if you fail to follow instructions again?"

These are important questions because they give you, the adult, a chance to not only gauge the child's understanding of what they did wrong but it also gives you the opportunity to provide appropriate behaviors that should be used instead.

This method takes patience and an emotional maturity that some adults don't possess. It can be very effective for children with behavioral issues, though.
